Last term one badly behaved client slowed lunch ordering for everyone. Design a rate limiter for the
               canteen ordering API. Say which algorithm you chose and what you rejected, give real numbers, and say what
               happens when the limiter's own storage is down. Measure it under the lunch peak before you hand it in.

<<<SOURCE 2 04a68a6e015c>>>
from: file rate-limiter-design.pdf, attached to Hand-in: Design rate limiting for the ordering API, section "When Redis is down", page 3
The limiter fails open: if Redis cannot be reached within 50 milliseconds, the request is allowed and a counter is incremented for the dashboard. Refusing every order because the limiter is broken would turn a small outage into a total one. The cost is that during a Redis outage nothing is limited, which I think is the right way round.
<<<END SOURCE 2 04a68a6e015c>>>

<<<SOURCE 3 04a68a6e015c>>>
from: file rate-limiter-design.pdf, attached to Hand-in: Design rate limiting for the ordering API, section "What I tested", page 3
A k6 script ran the lunch peak against a staging copy: 900 requests a minute from 300 virtual students, plus one client polling every 200 milliseconds. Without the limiter the p95 for placing an order was 2.4 seconds. With it, the polling client was refused about 94 per cent of the time and the p95 for everyone else came down to 310 milliseconds. No ordinary student in the test was ever refused.
<<<END SOURCE 3 04a68a6e015c>>>

<<<SOURCE 4 04a68a6e015c>>>
from: file rate-limiter-design.pdf, attached to Hand-in: Design rate limiting for the ordering API, section "What a limit has to do", page 1
It should stop one client hurting the others without refusing a student who is placing a normal order. A person tapping quickly should never notice it. It has to work across the two application instances behind the load balancer, so a counter in process memory is not enough: each instance would allow the full rate and the real limit would double whenever we scale.
<<<END SOURCE 4 04a68a6e015c>>>

Last term one badly behaved client slowed lunch ordering for everyone. Design a rate limiter for the
               canteen ordering API. Say which algorithm you chose and what you rejected, give real numbers, and say what

from: file rate-limiter-design.pdf, attached to Hand-in: Design rate limiting for the ordering API, section "When Redis is down", page 3
The limiter fails open: if Redis cannot be reached within 50 milliseconds, the request is allowed and a counter is incremented for the dashboard. Refusing every order because the limiter is broken would turn a small outage into a total one. The cost is that during a Redis outage nothing is limited, which I think is the right way round.
<<<END SOURCE 2 ef18ce50629e>>>

A k6 script ran the lunch peak against a staging copy: 900 requests a minute from 300 virtual students, plus one client polling every 200 milliseconds. Without the limiter the p95 for placing an order was 2.4 seconds. With it, the polling client was refused about 94 per cent of the time and the p95 for everyone else came down to 310 milliseconds. No ordinary student in the test was ever refused.
<<<END SOURCE 3 ef18ce50629e>>>

<<<SOURCE 4 ef18ce50629e>>>
from: file rate-limiter-design.pdf, attached to Hand-in: Design rate limiting for the ordering API, section "What a limit has to do", page 1
It should stop one client hurting the others without refusing a student who is placing a normal order. A person tapping quickly should never notice it. It has to work across the two application instances behind the load balancer, so a counter in process memory is not enough: each instance would allow the full rate and the real limit would double whenever we scale.
